query:
Two members of the group each made statements about why they pursue a particular pressing variant over others. One framed their motivation as purely about sound quality, explicitly rejecting financial logic. Who made that statement, and what distinguishes their reasoning from someone else in the same exchange who discussed pressing variants and market data?

Options:
C. Marcus
A. Tom
B. Raj
D. Elliot
context:
[1] (about=Tom, episodic, t0 @2025-09-14T14:06:00) The market price is beside the point. I did not buy it as an investment. I bought it because the A1 mastering is demonstrably superior and I wanted to hear it properly.
[2] (about=Raj, episodic, t0 @2025-09-14T14:07:00) Sure. Though the mastering data supports the price gap, so the two aren't unrelated. I track these things because it helps me decide which variant to prioritise when multiple copies surface at once.
[3] (about=Raj, episodic, t1 @2025-09-21T14:01:00) I want to bring something up while we're all here. I've been tracking Japanese pressings of progressive rock specifically -- Genesis, Yes, early Jethro Tull. The pressing quality data is consistent: Japanese pressings of certain albums outperform the UK originals on measured distortion, channel separation, and surface noise. Not my opinion. Measurable.
[4] (about=Elliot, episodic, t2 @2025-09-21T14:05:00) Japanese pressings trade at a premium on Discogs. 30-40% above UK equivalents in most categories I track. E
[5] (about=Tom, episodic, t2 @2025-09-21T14:02:00) Japanese pressings are manufactured for an export market with different sonic priorities. The frequency response is equalised differently. What you're measuring is not better quality -- it is a different tonal character.
[6] (about=Raj, episodic, t2 @2025-09-21T14:03:00) Technically the Japanese pressings were often cut from master tapes supplied directly by the label -- sometimes earlier generations than the ones used for subsequent UK pressings. That's not a preference. That's provenance.
[7] (about=Marcus, episodic, t2 @2025-09-21T14:04:00) Raj's point on the master tape generation is correct for some titles. I've seen the CBS Japanese pressings of Miles Davis sourced from first-generation lacquers that weren't used for UK pressings at all. It depends entirely on the specific title and the label's arrangement with their Japanese licensee.
[8] (about=Tom, episodic, t2 @2025-09-21T14:19:00) I will grant that the Japanese pressing performs well on this particular title. The Charisma pressing of this specific album has a known compression issue in the A-side cut. That does not constitute a general rule about Japanese pressings.
[9] (about=Raj, episodic, t8 @2025-10-12T14:33:00) Technically Talk Talk originals are one of the more expensive corners of the British post-punk market right now. Spirit of Eden UK first press tracks at £120 to £160 depending on condition. The Music on Vinyl version is £25. That is a meaningful cost-benefit calculation.
[10] (about=Tom, episodic, t7 @2025-10-12T14:00:00) I have been meaning to do this for some time. I have the original UK pressing of Spirit of Eden on Parlophone and a recent reissue on Music on Vinyl. I want to play the opening of side one on each. Without the comparison you cannot hear what is lost.
[11] (about=Carmen, core, t2 @2025-09-21T14:02:00) Carmen has avoided Japanese pressings for the jazz catalog on principle, feeling they are a step removed from the source, but may reconsider for specific titles based on this discussion.
[12] (about=GROUP, said_by=Dani, group-interaction, t2 @2025-09-21T14:02:00) After the comparison, Dani, Finn, and Nadia independently perceived the Japanese pressing as cleaner, less harsh in the high end, and more open, with the UK one having slight midrange compression.
[13] (about=Elliot, said_by=Raj, profile, t6 @2025-10-05T14:01:00) Raj points out Elliot has been arguing mono pressings for about two years, and his preference may have been formed on a phase-inverted stereo system that degraded stereo playback.
[14] (about=Marcus, core, t0 @2025-09-14T14:00:00) Notes some KPM pressings used Decca's pressing plant, indicating high pressing quality.
[15] (about=Marcus, core, t2 @2025-09-21T14:02:00) Marcus suggests Carmen investigate Japanese Blue Note pressings from the King label pressing plant in the mid-1970s, noting superior imaging on a few titles he compared on his setup.
[16] (about=Nadia, core, t10 @2025-10-19T14:01:00) Nadia notes Areito pressings are hard to find in good condition, and there is a CBS international pressing that is easier to source but sounds different, unsure which is better without comparing.
[17] (about=Priya, episodic, t3 @2025-09-28T14:02:00) ok so I found this at the Dutch dealer on Friday -- Cluster II, the original Brain pressing. I've been sitting on it since Friday honestly, didn't want to listen until I played it here
[18] (about=Raj, core, t2 @2025-09-21T14:02:00) Raj agrees the Japanese pressing advantage is not a general rule, holding for about 60% of prog titles he tested, with exceptions clustering around labels with strong internal mastering departments like Vertigo, Island, and some Charisma catalog outside Genesis.
[19] (about=Raj, core, t0 @2025-09-14T14:00:00) Uses market data to decide which variant to prioritise when multiple copies surface.
[20] (about=Tom, core, t0 @2025-09-14T14:00:00) Bought the A1 pressing for mastering quality, not as an investment; considers A1 mastering demonstrably superior.
[21] (about=Tom, core, t6 @2025-10-05T14:01:00) Tom holds that for certain Blue Note titles, the mono pressing is the artistically intended version and the stereo is an afterthought, independent of equipment.
[22] (about=GROUP, said_by=Tom, group-interaction, t18 @2025-11-16T14:01:00) Tom concedes that if a pressing is genuinely unique and a lossless option is available, the redundancy has some rational basis, though he would not do it himself.

query:
One group member confessed to buying digital copies of records as a form of backup. When asked what kind of digital files they used, their answer revealed a specific and principled approach to digital purchasing. Who gave this answer, and what in how they described their method distinguishes them from another member who also uses streaming and digital audio?

Options:
B. Finn
A. Dani
D. Priya
C. Raj
context:
[1] (about=Dani, episodic, t18 @2025-11-16T14:07:00) Bandcamp downloads mostly. where the artist sells lossless. I'm not ripping my own records, I don't have the setup. but for the shoegaze stuff especially -- some of these records are fragile and rare and if something happened I'd be gutted
[2] (about=Finn, episodic, t18 @2025-11-16T14:06:00) DANI 😂 what kind of digital? rips or downloads
[3] (about=Dani, episodic, t18 @2025-11-16T14:09:00) I know it's not a backup in a technical sense. it's more like... if the record gets destroyed at least I can still hear the music. which I think is a reasonable thing to want
[4] (about=Dani, episodic, t18 @2025-11-16T14:17:00) thank you finn. and I want to say I'm not replacing the vinyl with the file. it's the other way around -- the vinyl is still the main thing. the file is just there in case
[5] (about=Tom, episodic, t18 @2025-11-16T14:08:00) To be precise, what you are describing is not a backup. It is a parallel digital purchase. The vinyl and the file are separate objects. The file offers no insurance on the physical record.
[6] (about=Tom, episodic, t18 @2025-11-16T14:01:00) No. The vinyl is the recording. If a digital backup exists it is not the same object and the exercise is therefore redundant.
[7] (about=Priya, episodic, t17 @2025-11-16T14:00:00) ok today I want to talk about something slightly uncomfortable. has anyone started keeping digital backups of their collection? like rips or hi-res downloads alongside the vinyl
[8] (about=Raj, episodic, t18 @2025-11-16T14:02:00) I do not backup digitally. Streaming is for discovery now, vinyl is for listening. I don't have a use case for a rip when I can put the record on.
[9] (about=Marcus, episodic, t18 @2025-11-16T14:03:00) I have ripped a small number of records I consider irreplaceable -- things I would not be able to find again. Not for listening. As an archive. There's a distinction between preservation and playback.
[10] (about=Elliot, episodic, t18 @2025-11-16T14:04:00) 1. I have not. 2. Digital files require their own storage infrastructure. 3. The probability of record loss is lower than the probability of drive failure. My calculation says no. E
[11] (about=Elliot, core, t18 @2025-11-16T14:01:00) Elliot has not backed up digitally, calculating that the probability of record loss is lower than drive failure and the infrastructure cost outweighs the risk at most collection sizes, though he acknowledges the math might differ for Dani's specific catalog.
[12] (about=Raj, core, t14 @2025-11-02T14:01:00) Raj takes some offence at Dani's observation but admits it is not entirely wrong, and says he'd like to buy a copy if Nadia can recommend a dealer, which is a different kind of decision than he usually makes.
[13] (about=Tom, episodic, t0 @2025-09-14T14:18:00) Well, actually that depends on the condition grade. A VG copy at £3 is a reasonable find. A VG+ copy at £3 is exceptional. What is the condition?
